metadata.title: Have robotaxis hit a tipping point? Wall Street and experts are split.

content.text:
If you live in a major city, robotaxis are seemingly everywhere. You've probably seen one, know someone who's ridden in one, or even had a Waymo drive you somewhere. Most people are either enamored or terrified.
But the robotaxi tipping point may be upon us, though there are still a number of hurdles for the industry's major players to surmount before hailing a robotaxi on any US road becomes a reality.
"We're past the tipping point," Anthony Townsend, senior research associate at Cornell Tech and author of "Ghost Road: Beyond the Driverless Car," told Yahoo Finance. "Robotaxis are a technology that has become too big to fail."
But not everyone agrees.
Katie Driggs-Campbell, associate professor of electrical and computer engineering at the University of Illinois Grainger College of Engineering, said a true tipping point arrives when "these systems could really be deployed anywhere and everywhere and when it is safe to assume that most people have ridden in one."
That may be close in the Bay Area, she said, but "certainly not in Central Illinois." But robotaxi operators like Waymo and Tesla (TSLA) would like to change that — and fast. Here's where the robotaxi space stands.
Expansion everywhere
Take Alphabet's (GOOG, GOOGL) Waymo. The service operates in 15 US cities, and last month Waymo added nearly 250 square miles of service across five cities, including Torrance in Los Angeles, La Jolla in San Diego, and a connection to BART's Berryessa Station in the Bay Area. It also opened rides to everyone in San Antonio, San Diego, and Tampa, and added pickups at the Harry Reid International Airport in Las Vegas for existing riders.
But Waymo hit a major setback last week. California's DMV barred its robotaxis from the state's freeways, saying the driverless freeway operations pose an "imminent hazard to public safety" and citing "recurring incursions" by its vehicles into active construction zones.
Waymo responded by pulling its robotaxis off freeways in every US market where it offers them, saying it had "temporarily restricted freeway operations across our other operating markets to evaluate our performance." The likely path back is a software update, proof to regulators that the problem is fixed, and a relaunch.
Tesla started selling its driverless Cybercab to private buyers this month, but only to a hand-picked few, and only if they agree to a monthly fee on top of the sticker price. The two-seater, which has no steering wheel or pedals, costs $29,990 before taxes, with deliveries estimated for December. Buyers also put down a $1,000 nonrefundable deposit and sign up for a $299-per-month "Autonomy Subscription," with the first month free.
Musk revealed that Tesla plans to build a Model Y with no driver controls to enable robotaxi rides for larger groups of passengers.
JPMorgan analyst Rajat Gupta sees this as an early sign the self-driving bet is working. Tesla's rapid robotaxi ramp, "including this weekend's launch of customer Cybercab sales, is starting to present early validation of the company's unique advantage in physical AI," Gupta wrote in a note to clients Sunday.
Gupta expects customer-owned vehicles running unsupervised Full Self-Driving (FSD) to become "another, capital-light source of supply" for the network starting in the second quarter of 2027. Scale matters too, as JPMorgan ties 40% of its sum-of-the-parts Tesla valuation to robotaxis.
Tesla now has 1,306 registered robotaxis in Texas, compared with 1,321 for Waymo. But registrations aren't rides. JPMorgan estimates 690 Teslas are operating nationally without a safety driver, vs. 4,000 driverless Waymos logging 4 million miles a week, more than six times Tesla's 635,000.
Austin is where much of the robotaxi action is. Gupta estimates Tesla now accounts for half of all autonomous miles in the city, with a 440-square-mile service area versus Waymo's 150, despite launching unsupervised rides 10 months later. His model has Tesla matching Waymo's national weekly mileage in the second half of 2027 with a fleet of 18,000 robotaxis.
Barclays analyst Dan Levy upgraded Tesla to Overweight last month, citing in part "signs of Robotaxi inflection." He wrote, "Tesla appears to be starting the rapid scaling that investors had long been waiting for, especially in Austin," though he doesn't "expect Robotaxi to be financially material in the near/mid-term."
Tesla already operates its own robotaxi network of Cybercabs and Model Y SUVs in Austin, Dallas, Fort Worth, Houston, Miami, Orlando, San Antonio, and Tampa. And it is in those areas that personal Cybercabs will also operate.
"We view personal ownership as a complementary opportunity alongside Tesla's company-operated robotaxi fleet," Morgan Stanley analyst Andrew Percoco said in a note published this week. "Selling the vehicle allows customers to fund the hardware while Tesla generates recurring subscription revenue."
So who has the better technology? Experts lean Waymo, for now.
"Everyone knows Waymo's technology is better. But Tesla is much better at rapid improvement and scaling. It's their race to lose," Townsend said.
"Just based on the real-world experience and safety assessments, I think Waymo is likely safer and more reliable," Driggs-Campbell said.
Columbia Business School professor Len Sherman said, "None of the current providers has an optimal solution and insurmountable competitive advantage yet." Waymo has "an admirable safety record, but their current technology is much too expensive," while Tesla's tech "has yet to be fully proven."
"We're still in early innings of the robotaxi game," Sherman said.
Regulatory hurdles
"Local regulation is the biggest barrier right now, but that's a good thing," Townsend said. "This technology is far from perfect, and right now it's mostly a tool for perpetuating auto dependency. Big cities want to force taxibot companies to feed passengers to buses and train lines rather than compete with them, and to make roads safer for cyclists and pedestrians. I think they'll succeed."
The state-by-state patchwork slows things down, Driggs-Campbell said. Illinois is still working through its regulatory process, so Waymo's vehicles are only collecting data in Chicago.
Tesla has picked its battles accordingly. Per JPMorgan, Texas permits driverless operations through self-certification and vehicle registration, Florida requires no additional state-level authorization, and Nevada granted Tesla and others permission in August to operate up to 5,000 vehicles in Clark County (where Las Vegas is located). Together with Arizona, those states hold 20% of the US population.
Safety headlines are a separate problem. "Local media attention to robotaxi incidents is a very misleading gauge of actual AV safety performance," Sherman said. "Robotaxi vehicles are three to four times safer than human drivers on a per-mile basis, but are probably ten times more likely to receive media coverage for each safety incident."
What needs to happen for robotaxis to be ubiquitous
Rider demand isn't the main constraint. "Resistance to this technology fades quickly with exposure. But our expectations are also much higher than human drivers," Townsend said. Sherman pointed to survey data showing consumers "gain trust in AV technology shortly after their first ride."
"Supply side constraints will be far more important than consumer acceptance in pacing the growth of robotaxi services," Sherman said. That means companies devoting substantial capital to fleets, plus the charging, cleaning, and maintenance facilities that support them.
The tech isn't fully baked either. Driggs-Campbell said weather and mapping are still hurdles, and she's not sure the cost per ride has improved enough to make each trip profitable.
"The opportunity is meaningful, but the pace of adoption will depend on how useful — and economical — the vehicle becomes for everyday ownership," Morgan Stanley's Percoco said.
Tesla's first Cybercab owners will start testing that when deliveries begin next month.
